fields.rationale: Before body has await tx.markPaid(id) then await publish(id) inside the transaction callback. Contract 1: commits staged writes only after callback fulfillment. fields.rationale: Probe before.commit and before['publish-after'] are each paid=false, notifications=1, with rollback after publish.

fields.quote: If publication succeeded and the commit then failed, the payment rolled back while its notification remained visible. The supplied probe records exactly that outcome: an unpaid record and one notification. A publication error after external delivery could produce the same mismatch, because rejecting the callback rolled back only the database writes.
fields.rationale: before.commit: paid=false, notifications=1, events [begin, write, publish, rollback]. before['publish-after']: paid=false, notifications=1, same event shape. Contract 1: callback or commit rejection rolls back staged writes. Contract 2: publish rejection may happen after an externally visible notification. The unpaid-plus-one-notification sentence is scoped to the supplied probe, not generalized beyond it.

fields.quote: Wait for the commit, then publish
fields.rationale: After awaits the transaction, then awaits publish. Probe after.none.events is [begin, write, commit, publish].

fields.quote: That await completes after commit, not merely after markPaid. A write or commit rejection exits the function before publication. In the supplied in-memory results, a failed commit now leaves zero notifications. A publication rejection still rejects the function, but cannot undo the committed payment. The probes show both possibilities: rejection before delivery leaves zero notifications; rejection after delivery leaves one. The author describes payment and notification as atomic, but this code establishes ordering, not an all-or-nothing result.
fields.rationale: Contract 1: transaction fulfills after commit; callback or commit rejection rolls back and does not fulfill, so after never reaches publish. after.write and after.commit both have notifications=0; after.commit is explicitly zero. after['publish-before']: paid=true, notifications=0, errors [publish-before]. after['publish-after']: paid=true, notifications=1, errors [publish-after]. source.json body: the author says moving publish 'makes payment and notification atomic.' after.publish-before (paid without notification) and after.publish-after (committed payment plus visible notification while the function still rejects) are not all-or-nothing. Failed-commit zero notifications is scoped to in-memory results.

fields.quote: A stronger order, not guaranteed delivery
fields.rationale: After orders commit before publish (after.none.events). Contract 4: a process can stop between awaited operations; no durable outbox or background retry. after['publish-before'] is paid=true, notifications=0. The title matches that ordering-without-delivery-guarantee reading.

fields.quote: Failed payment transactions no longer trigger publication. A process stop between commit and publication can still leave a paid record without a notification; no durable outbox or background retry is supplied. Retrying after uncertain delivery can duplicate notifications. Idempotent markPaid protects the payment write, not delivery: both versions produce two notifications under concurrent calls in the probe. These results support the ordering change, not exactly-once delivery or atomicity.
fields.rationale: after.write and after.commit have notifications=0; publish sits after the transaction await. Process-stop and missing outbox/retry are contract 4 (not a process-kill probe; footer already says none was performed). Uncertain delivery: after['publish-after'] is paid=true, notifications=1, function rejected; contract 3 gives no delivery deduplication, so another after() call would publish again. Concurrent: before.concurrent.notifications=2 and after.concurrent.notifications=2; probe.mjs asserts idempotent writes do not deduplicate publication. The closing sentence limits the probes to ordering, which matches those results rather than claiming exactly-once or atomicity.
